name: Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve
blurb: Misty forest, mountain grassland and a toad that gives birth to live young.

tip.title: Thin the figs
tip.text: Figs and forest fruit feed bats, chimpanzees, hornbills, duikers and beetles. Cut the figs and watch the fruit eaters, then the leopard, respond.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Wild figs
nodes.desc: Fig trees fruit through the year in many tropical forests and are a food source for bats, birds and primates.

nodes.name: Stream algae
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae film on stones in the clear streams that drain the mountain springs.
A forest and swamp herbivore of West Africa, mostly in Liberia with small numbers in Guinea. It eats ferns, herbs and fallen fruit, and leopards take its young.
The Nimba area is known for chimpanzees that use stones as tools. They eat mostly fruit, including that of Guinea plum.

nodes.name: Stream insects
nodes.desc: Insect larvae and other small animals that graze algae and debris in the mountain streams.
The top predator of West African forests. Wikipedia lists it among the predators of young pygmy hippos.
The southern slopes are wetter than the northern ones. Mist and cloud feed the mossy forest on the ridge.
Thin ridge soils and the nutrients released from dead leaves feed the forest and grassland.

nodes.name: Dung beetles & fungi
nodes.desc: Large dung beetles such as Heliocopris are among the most recorded insects here. With fungi they recycle dead matter into soil.
